      - paragraph
        - StaticText "Born in London, Turing was raised in "

        - StaticText ", Britain's "

        - StaticText " centre that produced "
        - link "Ultra" [ref=e387]
        - StaticText " intelligence. He led "
        - link "Hut 8" [ref=e388]
        - StaticText ", the section responsible for German naval cryptanalysis. Turing devised techniques for speeding the breaking of German "

        - StaticText " method, an "

        - StaticText " at the "

        - StaticText " and became interested in "

        - StaticText ". An inquest determined his death as suicide, but the evidence is also consistent with accidental poisoning."

        - paragraph
          - StaticText "Atheist, homosexual, eccentric, marathon-running mathematician, A. M. Turing was in large part responsible not only for the concept of computers, incisive theorems about their powers, and a clear vision of the possibility of computer minds, but also for the cracking of German ciphers during the Second World War. It is fair to say we owe much to Alan Turing for the fact that we are not under Nazi rule today."

          - StaticText " an independent boarding school in the market town of "

          - StaticText " in Dorset, where he boarded at Westcott House. The first day of term coincided with the "

          - StaticText "Turing's natural inclination towards mathematics and science did not earn him respect from some of the teachers at Sherborne, whose "

          - StaticText " placed more emphasis on the "
          - link "classics" [ref=e582]

          - StaticText "Scientific Specialist"

          - superscript
            - link "[28]" [ref=e911]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "28"
                - StaticText "]"
          - StaticText " Despite this, Turing continued to show remarkable ability in the studies he loved, solving advanced problems in 1927 without having studied even elementary "
          - link "calculus" [ref=e583]
          - StaticText ". In 1928, aged 16, Turing encountered "
          - link "Albert Einstein" [ref=e584]
          - StaticText "'s work; not only did he grasp it, but it is possible that he managed to deduce Einstein's questioning of "

            - StaticText "I am sure I could not have found anywhere another companion so brilliant and yet so charming and unconceited. I regarded my interest in my work, and in such things as astronomy (to which he introduced me) as something to be shared with him and I think he felt a little the same about me ... I know I must put as much energy if not as much interest into my work as if he were alive, because that is what he would like me to do."

        - paragraph
          - StaticText "Turing's relationship with Morcom's mother continued long after Morcom's death, with her sending gifts to Turing, and him sending letters, typically on Morcom's birthday."

                - StaticText "51"
                - StaticText "]"
          - StaticText " A day before the third anniversary of Morcom's death (13 February 1933), he wrote to Mrs. Morcom:"
        - blockquote
          - paragraph
            - StaticText "I expect you will be thinking of Chris when this reaches you. I shall too, and this letter is just to tell you that I shall be thinking of Chris and of you tomorrow. I am sure that he is as happy now as he was when he was here. Your affectionate Alan."

        - paragraph

              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "53"
                - StaticText "]"
          - StaticText " Circa 1932, Turing wrote "
          - StaticText "The Nature of Spirit"
          - StaticText " while visiting Morcom's family home. His writings show a belief in such concepts as a spirit surviving death independent of the body. In a later letter, also written to Morcom's mother, Turing wrote:"
        - blockquote
          - paragraph
            - StaticText "Personally, I believe that spirit is really eternally connected with matter but certainly not by the same kind of body ... as regards the actual connection between spirit and body I consider that the body can hold on to a 'spirit', whilst the body is alive and awake the two are firmly connected. When the body is asleep I cannot guess what happens but when the body dies, the 'mechanism' of the body, holding the spirit is gone and the spirit finds a new body sooner or later, perhaps immediately."

      - region "University and work on computability" [ref=e160]
        - heading "University and work on computability" [level=3, ref=e424]
        - figure
          - link [ref=e596]
            - image
          - Figcaption
            - StaticText "Turing in the 1930s"
        - paragraph
          - StaticText "In 1929 Turing and his friend "
          - link "Christopher Morcom" [ref=e597]
          - StaticText " applied for scholarships at "
          - link "Trinity College, Cambridge" [ref=e598]
          - StaticText ". Morcom, who was successful, had various advantages over Turing – he was nearly a year older, and both his father and brother had studied at Trinity. However, he died three months after the offer was made. Turing, on the other hand, was unsuccessful, but sat the "
          - link "King's College, Cambridge" [ref=e599]
          - StaticText " Scholarship Examination in Mathematics in 1930. King's reserved most of its places for "
          - link "Etonians" [ref=e600]
          - StaticText " (there was a historic link with Eton as a feeder institution), making the exam very competitive for candidates from other schools. However, its examiners had a slightly different slant to those in other colleges."
          - superscript
            - link "[56]" [ref=e929]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "56"
                - StaticText "]"
          - StaticText " Hodges describes the King's examiners as looking for \"a spark of originality\" and notes that the papers were \"notorious for their unorthodox questions\"."
        - paragraph
          - StaticText "Turing was awarded an "
          - link "exhibition" [ref=e601]
          - StaticText " (a lower-value scholarship) worth £80 per annum (equivalent to about £4,300 as of 2023)."
          - superscript
            - link "[57]" [ref=e930]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "57"
                - StaticText "]"
          - superscript
            - link "[58]" [ref=e931]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "58"
                - StaticText "]"
          - StaticText " His undergraduate studies at Cambridge were from February 1931 to November 1934. He studied \"Schedule B\" of the "
          - link "Mathematical Tripos" [ref=e602]
          - StaticText " course."
          - superscript
            - link "[59]" [ref=e932]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "59"
                - StaticText "]"
          - StaticText " He was awarded first-class honours in mathematics. His dissertation, "
          - StaticText "On the Gaussian error function"
          - StaticText ", written during his senior year and delivered in November 1934 proved a version of the "
          - link "central limit theorem" [ref=e603]
          - StaticText ". It was finally accepted on 16 March 1935. By spring of that same year, Turing started his master's course ("
          - link "Part III" [ref=e604]
          - StaticText ")—which he completed in 1937—and, at the same time, he published his first paper, a one-page article called "
          - StaticText "Equivalence of left and right almost periodicity"
          - StaticText " (sent on 23 April), featured in the tenth volume of the "
          - link "Journal of the London Mathematical Society" [ref=e933]
          - StaticText "."
          - superscript
            - link "[60]" [ref=e934]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "60"
                - StaticText "]"
          - StaticText " Later that year, Turing was elected a "
          - link "Fellow" [ref=e605]
          - StaticText " of King's College on the strength of his dissertation"
          - superscript
            - link "[61]" [ref=e935]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "61"
                - StaticText "]"
          - StaticText " where he served as a lecturer."
          - superscript
            - link "[62]" [ref=e936]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "62"
                - StaticText "]"
          - StaticText " However, unknown to Turing, the version of the theorem he proved in his paper had already been proven by "
          - link "Jarl Waldemar Lindeberg" [ref=e606]
          - StaticText " in 1922. Despite this, the committee found Turing's methods original and so regarded the work worthy of consideration for the fellowship. "
          - link "Abram Besicovitch" [ref=e607]
          - StaticText "'s report for the committee went so far as to say that if Turing's work had been published before Lindeberg's, it would have been \"an important event in the mathematical literature of that year\"."
          - superscript
            - link "[63]" [ref=e937]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "63"
                - StaticText "]"
          - superscript
            - link "[64]" [ref=e938]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "64"
                - StaticText "]"
          - superscript
            - link "[65]" [ref=e939]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "65"
                - StaticText "]"
        - paragraph
          - StaticText "Between the springs of 1935 and 1936, at the same time as "
          - link "Alonzo Church" [ref=e608]
          - StaticText ", Turing worked on the decidability of problems, starting from "
          - link "Gödel's incompleteness theorems" [ref=e609]
          - StaticText ". In mid-April 1936, Turing sent "
          - link "Max Newman" [ref=e610]
          - StaticText " the first draft typescript of his investigations. That same month, Church published his "
          - StaticText "An Unsolvable Problem of Elementary Number Theory"
          - StaticText ", with similar conclusions to Turing's then-yet unpublished work. Finally, on 28 May of that year, he finished and delivered his 36-page paper for publication called \""
          - link "On Computable Numbers, with an Application to the Entscheidungsproblem" [ref=e611]
          - StaticText "\"."
          - superscript
            - link "[66]" [ref=e940]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["

                - StaticText "]"
          - superscript
            - link "[67]" [ref=e941]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "67"
                - StaticText "]"
          - StaticText " It was published in the "
          - StaticText "Proceedings of the London Mathematical Society"
          - StaticText " journal in two parts, the first on 30 November and the second on 23 December."
          - superscript
            - link "[68]" [ref=e942]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "68"
                - StaticText "]"
          - StaticText " In this paper, Turing proved results on the limits of computation, introducing the formal and simple hypothetical devices that became known as "
          - link "Turing machines" [ref=e612]
          - StaticText ". The "
          - link "Entscheidungsproblem" [ref=e943]
          - StaticText " (decision problem) was originally posed by German mathematician "
          - link "David Hilbert" [ref=e613]
          - StaticText " in 1928, and consists of seeking a computational procedure for proving or disproving theorems in the logical calculus employed by Hilbert. Turing argued that his \"computing machine\" would be capable of performing any conceivable mathematical computation if it were representable by finitary means (as an "
          - link "algorithm" [ref=e614]
          - StaticText "). He went on to prove that there was no solution to the "
          - StaticText "decision problem"
          - StaticText " by first showing that some variants of the "
          - link "halting problem" [ref=e615]
          - StaticText " for Turing machines are "
          - link "undecidable" [ref=e616]
          - StaticText ": in parcitular, it is not possible to decide algorithmically whether a Turing machine will produce an infinite output. This paper has been called \"easily the most influential math paper in history\"."
          - superscript
            - link "[69]" [ref=e944]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "69"
                - StaticText "]"
        - figure
          - link [ref=e617]
            - image
          - Figcaption
            - link "King's College, Cambridge" [ref=e945]
            - StaticText ", where Turing was an undergraduate in 1931 and became a Fellow in 1935. The computer room is named after him."
        - paragraph
          - StaticText "Although "
          - link "Turing's proof" [ref=e618]
          - StaticText " was published shortly after Church's equivalent proof using his "
          - link "lambda calculus" [ref=e619]
          - StaticText ","
          - superscript
            - link "[70]" [ref=e946]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "70"
                - StaticText "]"
          - StaticText " Turing's approach is considerably more accessible and intuitive than Church's."
          - superscript
            - link "[71]" [ref=e947]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "71"
                - StaticText "]"
          - StaticText " It also included a notion of a 'Universal Machine' (now known as a "
          - link "universal Turing machine" [ref=e620]
          - StaticText "), with the idea that such a machine could perform the tasks of any other computation machine (as indeed could Church's lambda calculus). According to the "
          - link "Church–Turing thesis" [ref=e621]
          - StaticText ", Turing machines and the lambda calculus are capable of computing anything that is computable. "
          - link "John von Neumann" [ref=e622]
          - StaticText " acknowledged that the central concept of the modern computer was due to Turing's paper."
          - superscript
            - link "[72]" [ref=e948]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "72"
                - StaticText "]"
          - StaticText " To this day, Turing machines are a central object of study in "
          - link "theory of computation" [ref=e623]

            - link "[73]" [ref=e949]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "73"
                - StaticText "]"
        - paragraph
          - StaticText "From September 1936 to July 1938, Turing spent most of his time studying under Church at "

          - StaticText ","
          - superscript
            - link "[5]" [ref=e950]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "5"
                - StaticText "]"
          - StaticText " in the second year as a "
          - link "Jane Eliza Procter Visiting Fellow" [ref=e625]
          - StaticText ". In addition to his purely mathematical work, he studied cryptology and also built three of four stages of an electro-mechanical "
          - link "binary multiplier" [ref=e626]
          - StaticText "."
          - superscript
            - link "[74]" [ref=e951]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["

          - StaticText " In June 1938, he obtained his PhD from the "

              - StaticText "citation needed"
            - StaticText "]"
          - StaticText " his dissertation, "
          - link "Systems of Logic Based on Ordinals" [ref=e953]
          - StaticText ","
          - superscript
            - link "[75]" [ref=e954]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "75"
                - StaticText "]"
          - superscript
            - link "[76]" [ref=e955]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["

    - region "Career and research" [ref=e138]
      - heading "Career and research" [level=2, ref=e161]
      - paragraph
        - StaticText "When Turing returned to Cambridge, he attended lectures given in 1939 by "
        - link "Ludwig Wittgenstein" [ref=e425]
        - StaticText " about the "
        - link "foundations of mathematics" [ref=e426]
        - StaticText "."

              - StaticText "]"

      - region "Cryptanalysis" [ref=e162]
        - heading "Cryptanalysis" [level=3, ref=e428]
        - paragraph
          - StaticText "During the Second World War, Turing was a leading participant in the breaking of German ciphers at "
          - link "Bletchley Park" [ref=e635]
          - StaticText ". The historian and wartime codebreaker "
          - link "Asa Briggs" [ref=e636]
          - StaticText " has said, \"You needed exceptional talent, you needed genius at Bletchley and Turing's was that genius.\""
          - superscript
            - link "[82]" [ref=e958]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "82"
                - StaticText "]"
        - paragraph
          - StaticText "From September 1938, Turing worked part-time with the "
          - link "Government Code and Cypher School" [ref=e637]
          - StaticText " (GC&CS), the British codebreaking organisation. He concentrated on "
          - link "cryptanalysis of the Enigma cipher machine" [ref=e638]
          - StaticText " used by "
          - link "Nazi Germany" [ref=e639]
          - StaticText ", together with "
          - link "Dilly Knox" [ref=e640]
          - StaticText ", a senior GC&CS codebreaker."
          - superscript
            - link "[83]" [ref=e959]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "83"
                - StaticText "]"
          - StaticText " Soon after the July 1939 meeting near "
          - link "Warsaw" [ref=e641]
          - StaticText " at which the "
          - link "Polish Cipher Bureau" [ref=e642]
          - StaticText " gave the British and French details of the wiring of "
          - link "Enigma machine's rotors" [ref=e643]
          - StaticText " and their method of decrypting "
          - link "Enigma machine" [ref=e644]
          - StaticText "'s messages, Turing and Knox developed a broader solution."
          - superscript
            - link "[84]" [ref=e960]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "84"
                - StaticText "]"
          - StaticText " The Polish method relied on an insecure "
          - link "indicator" [ref=e645]
          - StaticText " procedure that the Germans were likely to change, which they in fact did in May 1940. Turing's approach was more general, using "
          - link "crib-based decryption" [ref=e646]
          - StaticText " for which he produced the functional specification of the "
          - link "bombe" [ref=e647]
          - StaticText " (an improvement on the Polish "
          - link "Bomba" [ref=e648]
          - StaticText ")."
          - superscript
            - link "[85]" [ref=e961]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "85"
                - StaticText "]"
        - figure
          - link [ref=e649]
            - image
          - Figcaption
            - StaticText "Two cottages in the stable yard at "
            - link "Bletchley Park" [ref=e962]
            - StaticText ". Turing worked here in 1939 and 1940, before moving to "
            - link "Hut 8" [ref=e963]
            - StaticText "."
        - paragraph
          - StaticText "On 4 September 1939, the day after the UK declared war on Germany, Turing reported to Bletchley Park, the wartime station of GC&CS."
          - superscript
            - link "[86]" [ref=e964]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "86"
                - StaticText "]"
          - StaticText " Like all others who came to Bletchley, he was required to sign the "
          - link "Official Secrets Act" [ref=e650]
          - StaticText ", in which he agreed not to disclose anything about his work at Bletchley, with severe legal penalties for violating the Act."
          - superscript
            - link "[87]" [ref=e965]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "87"
                - StaticText "]"
        - paragraph
          - StaticText "Specifying the bombe was the first of five major cryptanalytical advances that Turing made during the war. The others were: deducing the indicator procedure used by the German navy; developing a statistical procedure dubbed "
          - link "Banburismus" [ref=e966]
          - StaticText " for making much more efficient use of the bombes; developing a procedure dubbed "
          - link "Turingery" [ref=e967]
          - StaticText " for working out the cam settings of the wheels of the "
          - link "Lorenz SZ 40/42" [ref=e651]
          - StaticText " ("
          - StaticText "Tunny"
          - StaticText ") cipher machine and, towards the end of the war, the development of a portable "
          - link "secure voice" [ref=e652]
          - StaticText " scrambler at "
          - link "Hanslope Park" [ref=e653]
          - StaticText " that was codenamed Delilah."
          - superscript
            - link "[88]" [ref=e968]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "88"
                - StaticText "]"
          - superscript
            - link "[89]" [ref=e969]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "89"
                - StaticText "]"
        - paragraph
          - StaticText "By using statistical techniques to optimise the trial of different possibilities in the code breaking process, Turing made an innovative contribution to the subject. He wrote two papers discussing mathematical approaches, titled "
          - StaticText "The Applications of Probability to Cryptography"
          - superscript
            - link "[90]" [ref=e970]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "90"
                - StaticText "]"
          - StaticText " and "
          - StaticText "Paper on Statistics of Repetitions"
          - StaticText ","
          - superscript
            - link "[91]" [ref=e971]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "91"
                - StaticText "]"
          - StaticText " which were of such value to GC&CS and its successor "
          - link "GCHQ" [ref=e654]
          - StaticText " that they were not released to the "
          - link "UK National Archives" [ref=e655]
          - StaticText " until April 2012, shortly before the centenary of his birth. A GCHQ mathematician, \"who identified himself only as Richard,\" said at the time that the fact that the contents had been restricted under the Official Secrets Act for some 70 years demonstrated their importance, and their relevance to post-war cryptanalysis:"
          - superscript
            - link "[92]" [ref=e972]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "92"
                - StaticText "]"
        - blockquote
          - paragraph
            - StaticText "[He] said the fact that the contents had been restricted \"shows what a tremendous importance it has in the foundations of our subject\". ... The papers detailed using \"mathematical analysis to try and determine which are the more likely settings so that they can be tried as quickly as possible\". ... Richard said that GCHQ had now \"squeezed the juice\" out of the two papers and was \"happy for them to be released into the public domain\"."
        - paragraph
          - StaticText "Turing had a reputation for eccentricity at Bletchley Park. He was known to his colleagues as \"Prof\" and his treatise on Enigma was known as the \"Prof's Book\"."
          - superscript
            - link "[93]" [ref=e973]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "93"
                - StaticText "]"
          - superscript
            - link "[94]" [ref=e974]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "94"
                - StaticText "]"
          - StaticText " According to historian "
          - link "Ronald Lewin" [ref=e656]
          - StaticText ", "
          - link "Jack Good" [ref=e657]
          - StaticText ", a cryptanalyst who worked with Turing, said of his colleague:"
        - blockquote
          - paragraph
            - StaticText "In the first week of June each year he would get a bad attack of hay fever, and he would cycle to the office wearing a service gas mask to keep the pollen off. His bicycle had a fault: the chain would come off at regular intervals. Instead of having it mended he would count the number of times the pedals went round and would get off the bicycle in time to adjust the chain by hand. Another of his eccentricities is that he chained his mug to the radiator pipes to prevent it being stolen."

              - link "[95]" [ref=e1146]
                - generic
                  - StaticText "["
                  - StaticText "95"
                  - StaticText "]"
        - paragraph
          - link "Peter Hilton" [ref=e658]
          - StaticText " recounted his experience working with Turing in "
          - link "Hut 8" [ref=e659]
          - StaticText " in his \"Reminiscences of Bletchley Park\" from "
          - StaticText "A Century of Mathematics in America:"
          - superscript
            - link "[96]" [ref=e975]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "96"
                - StaticText "]"
        - blockquote
          - paragraph
            - StaticText "It is a rare experience to meet an authentic genius. Those of us privileged to inhabit the world of scholarship are familiar with the intellectual stimulation furnished by talented colleagues. We can admire the ideas they share with us and are usually able to understand their source; we may even often believe that we ourselves could have created such concepts and originated such thoughts. However, the experience of sharing the intellectual life of a genius is entirely different; one realizes that one is in the presence of an intelligence, a sensibility of such profundity and originality that one is filled with wonder and excitement. Alan Turing was such a genius, and those, like myself, who had the astonishing and unexpected opportunity, created by the strange exigencies of the Second World War, to be able to count Turing as colleague and friend will never forget that experience, nor can we ever lose its immense benefit to us."
        - paragraph
          - StaticText "While working at Bletchley, Turing, who was a talented "

                - StaticText "]"

                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "98"
                - StaticText "]"
          - superscript
            - link "[99]" [ref=e978]

                - StaticText "["

                - StaticText "]"
          - StaticText " Turing tried out for the "
          - link "1948 British Olympic team" [ref=e661]
          - StaticText ", but he was hampered by an injury. His tryout time for the marathon was only 11 minutes slower than British silver medallist "
          - link "Thomas Richards" [ref=e662]

            - link "[100]" [ref=e979]

                - StaticText "100"
                - StaticText "]"
          - superscript

                - StaticText "]"
          - superscript
            - link "[102]" [ref=e981]

                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "102"
                - StaticText "]"
          - StaticText " When asked why he ran so hard in training he replied:"
        - blockquote
          - paragraph
            - StaticText "I have such a stressful job that the only way I can get it out of my mind is by running hard; it's the only way I can get some release."
            - superscript
              - link "[103]" [ref=e1147]
                - generic
                  - StaticText "["
                  - StaticText "103"
                  - StaticText "]"
        - paragraph
          - StaticText "Due to the challenges answering questions concerning what an outcome would have been if a historical event did or did not occur (the realm of "
          - link "counterfactual history" [ref=e663]
          - StaticText "), it is hard to estimate the precise effect Ultra intelligence had on the war."
          - superscript
            - link "[104]" [ref=e982]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "104"
                - StaticText "]"
          - StaticText " However, official war historian "
          - link "Harry Hinsley" [ref=e664]
          - StaticText " estimated that this work shortened the war in Europe by more than two years. He added the caveat that this did not account for the use of the atomic bomb and other eventualities."
          - superscript
            - link "[105]" [ref=e983]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "105"
                - StaticText "]"
        - paragraph
          - StaticText "At the end of the war, a memo was sent to all those who had worked at Bletchley Park, reminding them that the code of silence dictated by the Official Secrets Act did not end with the war but would continue indefinitely."
          - superscript
            - link "[87]" [ref=e984]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "87"
                - StaticText "]"
          - StaticText " Thus, even though Turing was appointed an "
          - link "Officer of the Order of the British Empire" [ref=e665]
          - StaticText " (OBE) in 1946 by King "
          - link "George VI" [ref=e666]
          - StaticText " for his wartime services, his work remained secret for many years."
          - superscript
            - link "[106]" [ref=e985]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "106"
                - StaticText "]"
          - superscript
            - link "[107]" [ref=e986]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "107"
                - StaticText "]"
      - region "Bombe" [ref=e163]
        - heading "Bombe" [level=3, ref=e429]
        - paragraph
          - StaticText "Within weeks of arriving at Bletchley Park,"
          - superscript
            - link "[86]" [ref=e987]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "86"
                - StaticText "]"
          - StaticText " Turing had specified an electromechanical machine called the "
          - link "bombe" [ref=e667]
          - StaticText ", which could break Enigma more effectively than the Polish "
          - link "bomba kryptologiczna" [ref=e988]
          - StaticText ", from which its name was derived. The bombe, with an enhancement suggested by mathematician "
          - link "Gordon Welchman" [ref=e668]
          - StaticText ", became one of the primary tools, and the major automated one, used to attack Enigma-enciphered messages."
          - superscript
            - link "[108]" [ref=e989]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "108"
                - StaticText "]"
        - figure
          - link [ref=e669]
            - image
          - Figcaption
            - StaticText "A working replica of a "
            - link "bombe" [ref=e990]
            - StaticText " now at "
            - link "The National Museum of Computing" [ref=e991]
            - StaticText " on Bletchley Park"
        - paragraph
          - StaticText "The bombe searched for possible correct settings used for an Enigma message (i.e., rotor order, rotor settings and plugboard settings) using a suitable "
          - link "crib" [ref=e992]
          - StaticText ": a fragment of probable "
          - link "plaintext" [ref=e670]
          - StaticText ". For each possible setting of the rotors (which had on the order of 10"
          - superscript
            - StaticText "19"
          - StaticText " states, or 10"
          - superscript
            - StaticText "22"
          - StaticText " states for the four-rotor U-boat variant),"
          - superscript
            - link "[109]" [ref=e993]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "109"
                - StaticText "]"
          - StaticText " the bombe performed a chain of logical deductions based on the crib, implemented "
          - link "electromechanically" [ref=e671]
          - StaticText "."
          - superscript
            - link "[110]" [ref=e994]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "110"
                - StaticText "]"
        - paragraph
          - StaticText "The bombe detected when a contradiction had occurred and ruled out that setting, moving on to the next. Most of the possible settings would cause contradictions and be discarded, leaving only a few to be investigated in detail. A contradiction would occur when an enciphered letter would be turned back into the same plaintext letter, which was impossible with the Enigma. The first bombe was installed on 18 March 1940."
          - superscript
            - link "[111]" [ref=e995]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "111"
                - StaticText "]"
        - region "Action This Day" [ref=e430]
          - heading "Action This Day" [level=4, ref=e672]
          - note
            - StaticText "Main article: "
            - link "Action This Day (memo)" [ref=e996]
          - paragraph
            - StaticText "By late 1941, Turing and his fellow cryptanalysts Welchman, "
            - link "Hugh Alexander" [ref=e997]
            - StaticText " and "
            - link "Stuart Milner-Barry" [ref=e998]
            - StaticText " were frustrated. Building on the "
            - link "work of the Poles" [ref=e999]
            - StaticText ", they had set up a good working system for decrypting Enigma signals, but their limited staff and bombes meant they could not translate all the signals. In the summer, they had considerable success, and shipping losses had fallen to under 100,000 tons a month; however, they badly needed more resources to keep abreast of German adjustments. They had tried to get more people and fund more bombes through the proper channels, but had failed."
            - superscript
              - link "[112]" [ref=e1148]
                - generic
                  - StaticText "["
                  - StaticText "112"
                  - StaticText "]"
          - paragraph
            - StaticText "On 28 October they wrote directly to "
            - link "Winston Churchill" [ref=e1000]
            - StaticText " explaining their difficulties, with Turing as the first named. They emphasised how small their need was compared with the vast expenditure of men and money by the forces and compared with the level of assistance they could offer to the forces."
            - superscript
              - link "[112]" [ref=e1149]
                - generic
                  - StaticText "["
                  - StaticText "112"
                  - StaticText "]"
            - StaticText " As "
            - link "Andrew Hodges" [ref=e1001]
            - StaticText ", biographer of Turing, later wrote, \"This letter had an electric effect.\""
            - superscript
              - link "[113]" [ref=e1150]
                - generic
                  - StaticText "["
                  - StaticText "113"
                  - StaticText "]"
            - StaticText " Churchill wrote a memo to "
            - link "General Ismay" [ref=e1002]
            - StaticText ", which read: \"ACTION THIS DAY. Make sure they have all they want on extreme priority and report to me that this has been done.\" On 18 November, the chief of the secret service reported that every possible measure was being taken."
            - superscript
              - link "[113]" [ref=e1151]
                - generic
                  - StaticText "["
                  - StaticText "113"
                  - StaticText "]"
            - StaticText " The cryptographers at Bletchley Park did not know of the Prime Minister's response, but as Milner-Barry recalled, \"All that we did notice was that almost from that day the rough ways began miraculously to be made smooth.\""
            - superscript
              - link "[114]" [ref=e1152]
                - generic
                  - StaticText "["
                  - StaticText "114"
                  - StaticText "]"
            - StaticText " More than two hundred bombes were in operation by the end of the war."
            - superscript
              - link "[115]" [ref=e1153]
                - generic
                  - StaticText "["
                  - StaticText "115"
                  - StaticText "]"
      - region "Hut 8 and the naval Enigma" [ref=e164]
        - heading "Hut 8 and the naval Enigma" [level=3, ref=e431]
        - figure
          - link [ref=e673]
            - image
          - Figcaption
            - StaticText "Statue of Turing holding an Enigma machine by "
            - link "Stephen Kettle" [ref=e1003]
            - StaticText " at Bletchley Park, commissioned by "
            - link "Sidney Frank" [ref=e1004]
            - StaticText ", built from half a million pieces of Welsh slate"
            - superscript
              - link "[116]" [ref=e1154]
                - generic
                  - StaticText "["
                  - StaticText "116"
                  - StaticText "]"
        - paragraph
          - StaticText "Turing decided to tackle the particularly difficult problem of cracking the "
          - link "German naval use of Enigma" [ref=e674]
          - StaticText " \"because no one else was doing anything about it and I could have it to myself\"."
          - superscript
            - link "[117]" [ref=e1005]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "117"
                - StaticText "]"
          - StaticText " In December 1939, Turing solved the essential part of the naval "
          - link "indicator" [ref=e675]
          - StaticText " system, which was more complex than the indicator systems used by the other services."
          - superscript
            - link "[117]" [ref=e1006]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "117"
                - StaticText "]"
          - superscript
            - link "[118]" [ref=e1007]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "118"
                - StaticText "]"
        - paragraph
          - StaticText "That same night, he also conceived of the idea of "
          - link "Banburismus" [ref=e1008]
          - StaticText ", a sequential statistical technique (what "
          - link "Abraham Wald" [ref=e676]
          - StaticText " later called "
          - link "sequential analysis" [ref=e677]
          - StaticText ") to assist in breaking the naval Enigma, \"though I was not sure that it would work in practice, and was not, in fact, sure until some days had actually broken\"."
          - superscript
            - link "[117]" [ref=e1009]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "117"
                - StaticText "]"
          - StaticText " For this, he invented a measure of weight of evidence that he called the "
          - link "ban" [ref=e1010]
          - StaticText ". "
          - StaticText "Banburismus"
          - StaticText " could rule out certain sequences of the Enigma rotors, substantially reducing the time needed to test settings on the bombes."
          - superscript
            - link "[119]" [ref=e1011]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "119"
                - StaticText "]"
          - StaticText " Later this sequential process of accumulating sufficient weight of evidence using decibans (one tenth of a ban) was used in "
          - link "cryptanalysis of the Lorenz cipher" [ref=e678]
          - StaticText "."
          - superscript
            - link "[120]" [ref=e1012]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "120"
                - StaticText "]"
        - paragraph
          - StaticText "Turing travelled to the United States in November 1942 and worked with US Navy cryptanalysts on the naval Enigma and bombe construction in Washington."
          - superscript
            - link "[121]" [ref=e1013]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "121"
                - StaticText "]"
          - superscript
            - link "[122]" [ref=e1014]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "122"
                - StaticText "]"
          - StaticText " He also visited their "
          - link "Computing Machine Laboratory" [ref=e679]
          - StaticText " in "
          - link "Dayton, Ohio" [ref=e680]
          - StaticText "."
          - superscript
            - link "[123]" [ref=e1015]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "123"
                - StaticText "]"
        - paragraph
          - StaticText "Turing's reaction to the American bombe design was far from enthusiastic:"
        - blockquote
          - paragraph
            - StaticText "The American Bombe programme was to produce 336 Bombes, one for each wheel order. I used to smile inwardly at the conception of Bombe hut routine implied by this programme, but thought that no particular purpose would be served by pointing out that we would not really use them in that way. Their test (of commutators) can hardly be considered conclusive as they were not testing for the bounce with electronic stop finding devices. Nobody seems to be told about rods or offiziers or banburismus unless they are really going to do something about it."
            - superscript
              - link "[124]" [ref=e1155]
                - generic
                  - StaticText "["
                  - StaticText "124"
                  - StaticText "]"
        - paragraph
          - StaticText "During this trip, he also assisted at "
          - link "Bell Labs" [ref=e681]
          - StaticText " with the development of "
          - link "secure speech" [ref=e682]
          - StaticText " devices."
          - superscript
            - link "[125]" [ref=e1016]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "125"
                - StaticText "]"
          - StaticText " He returned to Bletchley Park in March 1943. During his absence, "
          - link "Hugh Alexander" [ref=e683]
          - StaticText " had officially assumed the position of head of Hut 8, although Alexander had been "
          - StaticText "de facto"
          - StaticText " head for some time (Turing having little interest in the day-to-day running of the section). Turing became a general consultant for cryptanalysis at Bletchley Park."
          - superscript
            - link "[126]" [ref=e1017]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "126"
                - StaticText "]"
        - paragraph
          - StaticText "Alexander wrote of Turing's contribution:"
        - blockquote
          - paragraph
            - StaticText "There should be no question in anyone's mind that Turing's work was the biggest factor in Hut 8's success. In the early days, he was the only cryptographer who thought the problem worth tackling and not only was he primarily responsible for the main theoretical work within the Hut, but he also shared with Welchman and Keen the chief credit for the invention of the bombe. It is always difficult to say that anyone is 'absolutely indispensable', but if anyone was indispensable to Hut 8, it was Turing. The pioneer's work always tends to be forgotten when experience and routine later make everything seem easy and many of us in Hut 8 felt that the magnitude of Turing's contribution was never fully realised by the outside world."
            - superscript
              - link "[127]" [ref=e1156]
                - generic
                  - StaticText "["
                  - StaticText "127"
                  - StaticText "]"
      - region "Turingery" [ref=e165]
        - heading "Turingery" [level=3, ref=e432]
        - paragraph
          - StaticText "In July 1942, Turing devised a technique termed "
          - link "Turingery" [ref=e1018]
          - StaticText " (or jokingly "
          - generic
            - StaticText "Turingismus"
            - superscript
              - link "[128]" [ref=e1157]
                - generic
                  - StaticText "["
                  - StaticText "128"
                  - StaticText "]"
          - StaticText ") for use against the "
          - link "Lorenz cipher" [ref=e684]
          - StaticText " messages produced by the Germans' new "
          - StaticText "Geheimschreiber"
          - StaticText " (secret writer) machine. This was a "
          - link "teleprinter" [ref=e685]
          - link "rotor cipher attachment" [ref=e686]
          - StaticText " codenamed "
          - StaticText "Tunny"
          - StaticText " at Bletchley Park. Turingery was a method of "
          - StaticText "wheel-breaking"
          - StaticText ", i.e., a procedure for working out the cam settings of Tunny's wheels."
          - superscript
            - link "[129]" [ref=e1019]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "129"
                - StaticText "]"
          - StaticText " He also introduced the Tunny team to "
          - link "Tommy Flowers" [ref=e687]
          - StaticText " who, under the guidance of "
          - link "Max Newman" [ref=e688]
          - StaticText ", went on to build the "
          - link "Colossus computer" [ref=e689]
          - StaticText ", the world's first programmable digital electronic computer, which replaced a simpler prior machine (the "
          - link "Heath Robinson" [ref=e690]
          - StaticText "), and whose superior speed allowed the statistical decryption techniques to be applied usefully to the messages."
          - superscript
            - link "[130]" [ref=e1020]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "130"
                - StaticText "]"
          - StaticText " Some have mistakenly said that Turing was a key figure in the design of the Colossus computer. Turingery and the statistical approach of Banburismus undoubtedly fed into the thinking about "
          - link "cryptanalysis of the Lorenz cipher" [ref=e691]
          - StaticText ","
          - superscript
            - link "[131]" [ref=e1021]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "131"
                - StaticText "]"
          - superscript
            - link "[132]" [ref=e1022]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "132"
                - StaticText "]"
          - StaticText " but he was not directly involved in the Colossus development."
          - superscript
            - link "[133]" [ref=e1023]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "133"
                - StaticText "]"
      - region "Delilah" [ref=e166]
        - heading "Delilah" [level=3, ref=e433]
        - paragraph
          - StaticText "Following his work at "
          - link "Bell Labs" [ref=e692]
          - StaticText " in the US,"
          - superscript
            - link "[134]" [ref=e1024]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "134"
                - StaticText "]"
          - StaticText " Turing pursued the idea of electronic enciphering of speech in the telephone system. In the latter part of the war, he moved to work for the Secret Service's Radio Security Service (later "
          - link "HMGCC" [ref=e693]
          - StaticText ") at "
          - link "Hanslope Park" [ref=e694]
          - StaticText "."
          - superscript
            - link "[135]" [ref=e1025]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "135"
                - StaticText "]"
          - superscript
            - link "[136]" [ref=e1026]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "136"
                - StaticText "]"
          - StaticText " At the park, he further developed his knowledge of electronics with the assistance of "
          - link "REME" [ref=e695]
          - StaticText " officer Donald Bayley. Together they undertook the design and construction of a portable "
          - link "secure voice" [ref=e696]
          - StaticText " communications machine codenamed "
          - link "Delilah" [ref=e1027]
          - StaticText "."
          - superscript
            - link "[137]" [ref=e1028]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "137"
                - StaticText "]"
          - StaticText " The machine was intended for different applications, but it lacked the capability for use with long-distance radio transmissions. In any case, Delilah was completed too late to be used during the war. Though the system worked fully, with Turing demonstrating it to officials by encrypting and decrypting a recording of a "
          - link "Winston Churchill" [ref=e697]
          - StaticText " speech, Delilah was not adopted for use."
          - superscript
            - link "[138]" [ref=e1029]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "138"
                - StaticText "]"
          - StaticText " Turing also consulted with Bell Labs on the development of "
          - link "SIGSALY" [ref=e698]
          - StaticText ", a secure voice system that was used in the later years of the war."
      - region "Early computers and the Turing test" [ref=e167]
        - heading "Early computers and the Turing test" [level=3, ref=e434]
        - figure
          - link [ref=e699]
            - image
          - Figcaption
            - StaticText "Plaque, 78 High Street, "
            - link "Hampton" [ref=e1030]
        - paragraph
          - StaticText "Between 1945 and 1947, Turing lived in "
          - link "Hampton" [ref=e700]
          - StaticText ", London,"
          - superscript
            - link "[139]" [ref=e1031]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "139"
                - StaticText "]"
          - StaticText " while he worked on the design of the "
          - link "ACE" [ref=e701]
          - StaticText " (Automatic Computing Engine) at the "
          - link "National Physical Laboratory (NPL)" [ref=e702]
          - StaticText ". He presented a paper on 19 February 1946, which was the first detailed design of a "
          - link "stored-program computer" [ref=e703]
          - StaticText "."
          - superscript
            - link "[140]" [ref=e1032]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "140"
                - StaticText "]"
          - link "Von Neumann" [ref=e704]
          - StaticText "'s incomplete "
          - link "First Draft of a Report on the EDVAC" [ref=e1033]
          - StaticText " had predated Turing's paper, but it was much less detailed and, according to "
          - link "John R. Womersley" [ref=e705]
          - StaticText ", Superintendent of the NPL Mathematics Division, it \"contains a number of ideas which are Dr. Turing's own\"."
          - superscript
            - link "[141]" [ref=e1034]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "141"
                - StaticText "]"
        - paragraph
          - StaticText "Although ACE was a feasible design, the effect of the "
          - link "Official Secrets Act" [ref=e706]
          - StaticText " surrounding the wartime work at Bletchley Park made it impossible for Turing to explain the basis of his analysis of how a computer installation involving human operators would work."
          - superscript
            - link "[142]" [ref=e1035]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "142"
                - StaticText "]"
          - StaticText " This led to delays in starting the project and he became disillusioned. In late 1947 he returned to Cambridge for a sabbatical year during which he produced a seminal work on "
          - StaticText "Intelligent Machinery"
          - StaticText " that was not published in his lifetime."
          - superscript
            - link "[143]" [ref=e1036]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "143"
                - StaticText "]"
          - StaticText " While he was at Cambridge, the "
          - link "Pilot ACE" [ref=e707]
          - StaticText " was being built in his absence. It executed its first program on 10 May 1950, and a number of later computers around the world owe much to it, including the "
          - link "English Electric DEUCE" [ref=e708]
          - StaticText " and the American "
          - link "Bendix G-15" [ref=e709]
          - StaticText ". The full version of Turing's ACE was not built until after his death."
          - superscript
            - link "[144]" [ref=e1037]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "144"
                - StaticText "]"
        - paragraph
          - StaticText "According to the memoirs of the German computer pioneer "
          - link "Heinz Billing" [ref=e710]
          - StaticText " from the "
          - link "Max Planck Institute for Physics" [ref=e711]
          - StaticText ", published by Genscher, Düsseldorf, there was a meeting between Turing and "
          - link "Konrad Zuse" [ref=e712]
          - StaticText "."
          - superscript
            - link "[145]" [ref=e1038]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "145"
                - StaticText "]"
          - StaticText " It took place in "
          - link "Göttingen" [ref=e713]
          - StaticText " in 1947. The interrogation had the form of a colloquium. Participants were Womersley, Turing, Porter from England and a few German researchers like Zuse, Walther, and Billing (for more details see Herbert Bruderer, "
          - StaticText "Konrad Zuse und die Schweiz"
          - StaticText ")."
        - figure
          - link [ref=e714]
            - image
          - Figcaption
            - StaticText "A "
            - link "blue plaque" [ref=e1039]
            - StaticText " commemorating Alan Turing's work at the "
            - link "University of Manchester" [ref=e1040]
            - StaticText " where he was a "
            - link "Reader" [ref=e1041]
            - StaticText " from 1948 to 1954"
        - paragraph
          - StaticText "In 1948, Turing was appointed "
          - link "reader" [ref=e715]
          - StaticText " in the "
          - link "Mathematics Department" [ref=e716]
          - StaticText " at the "
          - link "University of Manchester" [ref=e717]
          - StaticText ". He lived at \"Copper Folly\", 43 Adlington Road, in "
          - link "Wilmslow" [ref=e718]
          - StaticText "."
          - superscript
            - link "[146]" [ref=e1042]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "146"
                - StaticText "]"
          - StaticText " A year later, he became deputy director of the Computing Machine Laboratory, where he worked on software for one of the earliest "
          - link "stored-program" [ref=e719]
          - StaticText " computers—the "
          - link "Manchester Mark 1" [ref=e720]
          - StaticText ". Turing wrote the first version of the Programmer's Manual for this machine, was elected to membership of the "
          - link "Manchester Literary and Philosophical Society" [ref=e721]
          - StaticText ","
          - superscript
            - link "[147]" [ref=e1043]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "147"
                - StaticText "]"
          - superscript
            - link "[148]" [ref=e1044]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "148"
                - StaticText "]"
          - StaticText " and was recruited by Ferranti as a consultant in the development of their commercialised machine, the Ferranti Mark 1. He continued to be paid consultancy fees by Ferranti until his death."
          - superscript
            - link "[149]" [ref=e1045]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "149"
                - StaticText "]"
          - StaticText " During this time, he continued to do more abstract work in mathematics,"
          - superscript
            - link "[150]" [ref=e1046]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "150"
                - StaticText "]"
          - StaticText " and in \""
          - link "Computing Machinery and Intelligence" [ref=e722]
          - StaticText "\","
          - superscript
            - link "[151]" [ref=e1047]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "151"
                - StaticText "]"
          - StaticText " Turing addressed the problem of "
          - link "artificial intelligence" [ref=e723]
          - StaticText ", and proposed an experiment that became known as the "
          - link "Turing test" [ref=e724]
          - StaticText ", an attempt to define a standard for a machine to be called \"intelligent\". The idea was that a computer could be said to \"think\" if a human interrogator could not tell it apart, through conversation, from a human being."
          - superscript
            - link "[152]" [ref=e1048]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "152"
                - StaticText "]"
          - StaticText " In the paper, Turing suggested that rather than building a program to simulate the adult mind, it would be better to produce a simpler one to simulate a child's mind and then to subject it to a course of education. A "
          - link "reversed" [ref=e725]
          - StaticText " form of the Turing test is widely used on the Internet; the "
          - link "CAPTCHA" [ref=e726]
          - StaticText " test is intended to determine whether the user is a human or a computer."
        - paragraph
          - StaticText "In 1948, Turing, working with his former undergraduate colleague, "
          - link "D.G. Champernowne" [ref=e727]
          - StaticText ", began writing a "
          - link "chess" [ref=e728]
          - StaticText " program for a computer that did not yet exist. By 1950, the program was completed and dubbed the "
          - link "Turochamp" [ref=e729]
          - StaticText "."
          - superscript
            - link "[85]" [ref=e1049]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "85"
                - StaticText "]"
          - StaticText " In 1952, he tried to implement it on a "
          - link "Ferranti Mark 1" [ref=e730]
          - StaticText ", but lacking enough power, the computer was unable to execute the program. Instead, Turing \"ran\" the program by flipping through the pages of the algorithm and carrying out its instructions on a chessboard, taking about half an hour per move. The game was recorded."
          - superscript
            - link "[153]" [ref=e1050]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "153"
                - StaticText "]"
          - StaticText " According to "
          - link "Garry Kasparov" [ref=e731]
          - StaticText ", Turing's program \"played a recognizable game of chess\"."
          - superscript
            - link "[154]" [ref=e1051]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "154"
                - StaticText "]"
          - StaticText " The program lost to Turing's colleague "
          - link "Alick Glennie" [ref=e732]
          - StaticText ", although it is said that it won a game against Champernowne's wife, Isabel."
          - superscript
            - link "[155]" [ref=e1052]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "155"
                - StaticText "]"
        - paragraph
          - StaticText "His Turing test was a significant, characteristically provocative, and lasting contribution to the debate regarding artificial intelligence, which continues after more than half a century."
          - superscript
            - link "[156]" [ref=e1053]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "156"
                - StaticText "]"
      - region "Pattern formation and mathematical biology" [ref=e168]
        - heading "Pattern formation and mathematical biology" [level=3, ref=e435]
        - paragraph
          - StaticText "When Turing was 39 years old in 1951, he turned to "
          - link "mathematical biology" [ref=e733]
          - StaticText ", finally publishing his masterpiece \""
          - link "The Chemical Basis of Morphogenesis" [ref=e734]
          - StaticText "\" in January 1952. He was interested in "
          - link "morphogenesis" [ref=e735]
          - StaticText ", the development of patterns and shapes in biological organisms. He suggested that a system of chemicals reacting with each other and diffusing across space, termed a "
          - link "reaction–diffusion system" [ref=e736]
          - StaticText ", could account for \"the main phenomena of morphogenesis\"."
          - superscript
            - link "[157]" [ref=e1054]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "157"
                - StaticText "]"
          - StaticText " He used systems of "
          - link "partial differential equations" [ref=e737]
          - StaticText " to model catalytic chemical reactions. For example, if a catalyst A is required for a certain chemical reaction to take place, and if the reaction produced more of the catalyst A, then we say that the reaction is "
          - link "autocatalytic" [ref=e738]
          - StaticText ", and there is positive feedback that can be modelled by nonlinear differential equations. Turing discovered that patterns could be created if the chemical reaction not only produced catalyst A, but also produced an inhibitor B that slowed down the production of A. If A and B then diffused through the container at different rates, then you could have some regions where A dominated and some where B did. To calculate the extent of this, Turing would have needed a powerful computer, but these were not so freely available in 1951, so he had to use linear approximations to solve the equations by hand. These calculations gave the right qualitative results, and produced, for example, a uniform mixture that oddly enough had regularly spaced fixed red spots. The Russian biochemist "
          - link "Boris Belousov" [ref=e739]
          - StaticText " had performed experiments with similar results, but could not get his papers published because of the contemporary prejudice that any such thing violated the "
          - link "second law of thermodynamics" [ref=e740]
          - StaticText ". Belousov was not aware of Turing's paper in the "
          - link "Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society" [ref=e1055]
          - StaticText "."
          - superscript
            - link "[158]" [ref=e1056]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "158"
                - StaticText "]"
        - paragraph
          - StaticText "Although published before the structure and role of "
          - link "DNA" [ref=e741]
          - StaticText " was understood, Turing's work on morphogenesis remains relevant today and is considered a seminal piece of work in mathematical biology."
          - superscript
            - link "[159]" [ref=e1057]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "159"
                - StaticText "]"
          - StaticText " Some of this work aimed to understand plant "
          - link "phyllotaxy" [ref=e742]
          - StaticText ", specifically how plant "
          - link "primordia" [ref=e743]
          - StaticText " form in a ring around the apical "
          - link "meristem" [ref=e744]
          - StaticText " during plant growth and development, forming Fibonacci series."
          - superscript
            - link "[160]" [ref=e1058]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "160"
                - StaticText "]"
          - StaticText " One of the early applications of Turing's paper was the work by James Murray explaining spots and stripes on the fur of cats, large and small."
          - superscript
            - link "[161]" [ref=e1059]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "161"
                - StaticText "]"
          - superscript
            - link "[162]" [ref=e1060]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "162"
                - StaticText "]"
          - superscript
            - link "[163]" [ref=e1061]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "163"
                - StaticText "]"
          - StaticText " Further research in the area suggests that Turing's work can partially explain the growth of \"feathers, hair follicles, the branching pattern of lungs, and even the left-right asymmetry that puts the heart on the left side of the chest\"."
          - superscript
            - link "[164]" [ref=e1062]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "164"
                - StaticText "]"
          - StaticText " In 2012, Sheth, et al. found that in mice, removal of "
          - link "Hox genes" [ref=e745]
          - StaticText " causes an increase in the number of digits without an increase in the overall size of the limb, suggesting that Hox genes control digit formation by tuning the wavelength of a Turing-type mechanism."
          - superscript
            - link "[165]" [ref=e1063]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "165"
                - StaticText "]"
          - StaticText " Later papers were not available until "
          - generic
            - StaticText "Collected Works of A."
            - StaticText "M."
            - StaticText "Turing"
          - StaticText " was published in 1992."
          - superscript
            - link "[166]" [ref=e1064]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "166"
                - StaticText "]"
        - paragraph
          - StaticText "A study conducted in 2023 confirmed Turing's mathematical model hypothesis. Presented by the "
          - link "American Physical Society" [ref=e746]
          - StaticText ", the experiment involved growing "
          - link "chia seeds" [ref=e747]
          - StaticText " in even layers within trays, later adjusting the available moisture. Researchers experimentally tweaked the factors which appear in the Turing equations, and, as a result, patterns resembling those seen in natural environments emerged. This is believed to be the first time that experiments with living vegetation have verified Turing's mathematical insight."
          - superscript
            - link "[167]" [ref=e1065]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "167"
                - StaticText "]"
          - superscript
            - link "[168]" [ref=e1066]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "168"
                - StaticText "]"
      - region "Ratio Club and other cybernetics contacts" [ref=e169]
        - heading "Ratio Club and other cybernetics contacts" [level=3, ref=e436]
        - paragraph
          - StaticText "The "
          - link "Ratio Club" [ref=e748]
          - StaticText " was a London "
          - link "dining club" [ref=e749]
          - StaticText " for researchers (mostly biologists) with interests in "
          - link "cybernetics" [ref=e750]
          - StaticText " (which encompassed "
          - link "neuroscience" [ref=e751]
          - StaticText ", artificial intelligence and computing), \"undoubtedly the most intellectually powerful grouping of British scientists interested in cybernetics\" according to "
          - link "Phil Husbands" [ref=e752]
          - StaticText " and "
          - link "Owen Holland" [ref=e753]
          - StaticText "."
          - superscript
            - link "[169]" [ref=e1067]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "169"
                - StaticText "]"
          - StaticText " At the first meeting on 4 September 1949 it was agreed to invite Turing to join. He accepted, giving his introductory talk at the 21 April 1950 meeting."
          - superscript
            - link "[note 2]" [ref=e1068]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "note 2"
                - StaticText "]"
          - superscript
            - link "[171]" [ref=e1069]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "171"
                - StaticText "]"
          - StaticText " He gave later talks based on both his \"Computing Machinery and Intelligence\" and \"Chemical Basis of Morphogenesis\" papers."
          - superscript
            - link "[170]" [ref=e1070]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "170"
                - StaticText "]"
        - paragraph
          - StaticText "On a 1949 visit to Britain to attend a conference on psychiatry American cybernetician "
          - link "Warren McCulloch" [ref=e754]
          - StaticText " made a trip to Manchester to meet Turing (who may have been unimpressed)."
          - superscript
            - link "[172]" [ref=e1071]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "172"
                - StaticText "]"
    - region "Personal life" [ref=e139]
      - heading "Personal life" [level=2, ref=e170]
      - region "Treasure" [ref=e171]
        - heading "Treasure" [level=3, ref=e437]
        - paragraph
          - StaticText "In the 1940s, Turing became worried about losing his savings in the event of a German invasion. To protect it, he bought two "
          - link "silver bars" [ref=e755]
          - StaticText " weighing "
          - StaticText "3,200"
          - StaticText " oz (90 kg) and worth £250 (in 2022, £8,000 "
          - link "adjusted for inflation" [ref=e756]
          - StaticText ", £48,000 at spot price) and buried them in a wood near Bletchley Park."
          - superscript
            - link "[173]" [ref=e1072]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "173"
                - StaticText "]"
          - StaticText " Upon returning to dig them up, Turing found that he was unable to break his own code describing where exactly he had hidden them. This, along with the fact that the area had been renovated, meant that he never regained the silver."
          - superscript
            - link "[174]" [ref=e1073]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "174"
                - StaticText "]"
      - region "Engagement" [ref=e172]
        - heading "Engagement" [level=3, ref=e438]
        - paragraph
          - StaticText "In 1941, Turing proposed marriage to Hut 8 colleague "
          - link "Joan Clarke" [ref=e757]
          - StaticText ", a fellow mathematician and cryptanalyst, but their engagement was short-lived. After admitting his homosexuality to his fiancée, who was reportedly \"unfazed\" by the revelation, Turing decided that he could not go through with the marriage."
          - superscript
            - link "[175]" [ref=e1074]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "175"
                - StaticText "]"
      - region "Chess" [ref=e173]
        - heading "Chess" [level=3, ref=e439]
        - paragraph
          - StaticText "Turing invented a hybrid chess sport, earlier than "
          - link "chess boxing" [ref=e758]
          - StaticText ", referred to as "
          - StaticText "round-the-house chess"
          - StaticText ", one player makes a chess move, then that player runs around the house, and the other player must make a chess move before the first player returns."
          - superscript
            - link "[176]" [ref=e1075]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "176"
                - StaticText "]"
          - superscript
            - link "[177]" [ref=e1076]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "177"
                - StaticText "]"
      - region "Homosexuality and indecency conviction" [ref=e174]
        - heading "Homosexuality and indecency conviction" [level=3, ref=e440]
        - figure
          - link [ref=e759]
            - image
          - Figcaption
            - StaticText "The "
            - link "Dancehouse Theatre" [ref=e1077]
            - StaticText ", formerly the Regal Cinema, pictured in 2006, outside of which Turing met Arnold Murray"
        - figure
          - link [ref=e760]
            - image
          - Figcaption
            - StaticText "The house where Alan Turing lived in his final years from 1950 to 1954 at 43 Adlington Road in "
            - link "Wilmslow" [ref=e1078]
        - paragraph
          - StaticText "In December 1951, Turing met Arnold Murray, a 19-year-old unemployed man. Turing was walking along Manchester's "
          - link "Oxford Road" [ref=e761]
          - StaticText " when he met Murray just outside the "
          - link "Regal Cinema" [ref=e762]
          - StaticText " and invited him to lunch. The two agreed to meet again and in January 1952 began an intimate relationship."
          - superscript
            - link "[178]" [ref=e1079]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "178"
                - StaticText "]"
          - StaticText " On 23 January, Turing's house in Wilmslow was burgled. Murray told Turing that he and the burglar were acquainted, and Turing reported the crime to the police. During the investigation, he acknowledged a sexual relationship with Murray. Homosexual acts were criminal offences in the United Kingdom at that time,"
          - superscript
            - link "[179]" [ref=e1080]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "179"
                - StaticText "]"
          - StaticText " and both men were charged with \""
          - link "gross indecency" [ref=e763]
          - StaticText "\" under "
          - link "Section 11" [ref=e764]
          - StaticText " of the "
          - link "Criminal Law Amendment Act 1885" [ref=e765]
          - StaticText "."
          - superscript
            - link "[180]" [ref=e1081]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "180"
                - StaticText "]"
          - StaticText " Initial "
          - link "committal proceedings" [ref=e766]
          - StaticText " for the trial were held on 27 February during which Turing's solicitor \"reserved his defence\", i.e., did not argue or provide evidence against the allegations. The proceedings were held at the "
          - link "Sessions House" [ref=e767]
          - StaticText " in "
          - link "Knutsford" [ref=e768]
          - StaticText "."
          - superscript
            - link "[181]" [ref=e1082]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "181"
                - StaticText "]"
        - paragraph
          - StaticText "Turing was later convinced by the advice of his brother and his own solicitor, and he entered a plea of guilty."
          - superscript
            - link "[182]" [ref=e1083]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "182"
                - StaticText "]"
          - StaticText " The case, "
          - generic
            - link "Regina" [ref=e1084]
            - StaticText " v. Turing and Murray,"
          - StaticText " was brought to trial on 31 March 1952."
          - superscript
            - link "[183]" [ref=e1085]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "183"
                - StaticText "]"
          - StaticText " Turing's barrister pushed for him not to be incarcerated, and he was sentenced to 12 months' probation."
          - superscript
            - link "[184]" [ref=e1086]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "184"
                - StaticText "]"
          - StaticText " His probation would be conditional on his agreement to undergo organotherapy or '"
          - link "chemical castration" [ref=e769]
          - StaticText "' in the "
          - link "Manchester Royal Infirmary" [ref=e770]
          - StaticText ", a process which induces "
          - link "hormonal" [ref=e771]
          - StaticText " physical changes with the aim of reducing "
          - link "libido" [ref=e772]
          - StaticText "."
          - superscript
            - link "[184]" [ref=e1087]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "184"
                - StaticText "]"
          - superscript
            - link "[185]" [ref=e1088]
