              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "185"
                - StaticText "]"
          - StaticText " In a letter, Turing wrote that \"no doubt I shall emerge from it all a different man, but quite who I've not found out\"."
          - superscript
            - link "[186]" [ref=e1089]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "186"
                - StaticText "]"
          - superscript
            - link "[187]" [ref=e1090]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "187"
                - StaticText "]"
          - StaticText " Murray was given a conditional discharge."
          - superscript
            - link "[188]" [ref=e1091]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "188"
                - StaticText "]"
          - StaticText " Turing was given injections of what was then called "
          - link "stilboestrol" [ref=e773]
          - StaticText " (now known as "
          - link "diethylstilbestrol" [ref=e774]
          - StaticText " or DES), a synthetic "
          - link "oestrogen" [ref=e775]
          - StaticText ". The treatment rendered him "
          - link "impotent" [ref=e776]
          - StaticText " and caused "
          - link "breast tissue to form" [ref=e777]
          - StaticText ", the latter of which Turing found somewhat amusing according to his friends."
          - superscript
            - link "[184]" [ref=e1092]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "184"
                - StaticText "]"
          - superscript
            - link "[189]" [ref=e1093]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "189"
                - StaticText "]"
          - StaticText " The hormonal injections did not appear to have worked as expected, as Turing was still finding himself attracted to men."
          - superscript
            - link "[184]" [ref=e1094]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "184"
                - StaticText "]"
        - paragraph
          - StaticText "Turing's conviction led to the removal of his security clearance and barred him from continuing with his cryptographic consultancy for "
          - link "GCHQ" [ref=e778]
          - StaticText ", the British "
          - link "signals intelligence" [ref=e779]
          - StaticText " agency that had evolved from GC&CS in 1946, though he kept his academic post. His trial took place only months after the defection to the Soviet Union of "
          - link "Guy Burgess" [ref=e780]
          - StaticText " and "
          - link "Donald Maclean" [ref=e781]
          - StaticText ", in summer 1951, after which the Foreign Office started to consider anyone known to be homosexual as a potential security risk."
          - superscript
            - link "[190]" [ref=e1095]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "190"
                - StaticText "]"
        - paragraph
          - StaticText "Turing was denied entry into the United States after his conviction in 1952, but was free to visit other European countries."
          - superscript
            - link "[191]" [ref=e1096]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "191"
                - StaticText "]"
          - StaticText " In the summer of 1952 he visited Norway, which was more tolerant of homosexuals. Among the various men he met there was one named Kjell Carlson. Kjell intended to visit Turing in the UK, but the authorities intercepted Kjell's postcard detailing his travel arrangements and were able to intercept and deport him before the two could meet."
          - superscript
            - link "[192]" [ref=e1097]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "192"
                - StaticText "]"
          - StaticText " It was also during this time that Turing started consulting a psychiatrist, Franz Greenbaum, with whom he got on well and who subsequently became a family friend."
          - superscript
            - link "[192]" [ref=e1098]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "192"
                - StaticText "]"
          - superscript
            - link "[193]" [ref=e1099]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "193"
                - StaticText "]"
        - region "\"Pryce's Buoy\"" [ref=e441]
          - heading "\"Pryce's Buoy\"" [level=4, ref=e782]
            - StaticText "\"Pryce's Buoy\""
          - paragraph
            - StaticText "Circa 1953, Turing wrote an unfinished comedic gay short story titled \"Pryce's Buoy\", which was unearthed in July 2026. It was notable for revealing his \"playful side\"."
            - superscript
              - link "[194]" [ref=e1158]
                - generic
                  - StaticText "["
                  - StaticText "194"
                  - StaticText "]"
            - superscript
              - link "[195]" [ref=e1159]
                - generic
                  - StaticText "["
                  - StaticText "195"
                  - StaticText "]"
            - StaticText " Largely autobiographical, the narrative piece detailed an erotic encounter between a male youth in need of money and a wealthy older theoretical scientist looking for casual sex."
            - superscript
              - link "[196]" [ref=e1160]
                - generic
                  - StaticText "["
                  - StaticText "196"
                  - StaticText "]"
            - StaticText " The title is a sexual "
            - link "pun" [ref=e1100]
            - StaticText " of a fictional math equation, described by Turing within the story, sharing similarities with the "
            - link "Turing test" [ref=e1101]
            - StaticText ". Literature professor Sarah Dillon of "
            - link "Cambridge University" [ref=e1102]
            - StaticText " unearthed the story in 2026 by transcribing Turing's handwritten prose from archived pages and researching its origins and intent."
            - superscript
              - link "[197]" [ref=e1161]
                - generic
                  - StaticText "["
                  - StaticText "197"
                  - StaticText "]"
            - StaticText " The story revealed a sense of humour that was not widely known prior; multiple news outlets reported that Turing was \"cheeky, funny, and really liked sex\"."
            - superscript
              - link "[198]" [ref=e1162]
                - generic
                  - StaticText "["
                  - StaticText "198"
                  - StaticText "]"
            - superscript
              - link "[199]" [ref=e1163]
                - generic
                  - StaticText "["
                  - StaticText "199"
                  - StaticText "]"
    - region "Death" [ref=e140]
      - heading "Death" [level=2, ref=e175]
      - figure
        - link [ref=e442]
          - image
        - Figcaption
          - StaticText "A "
          - link "blue plaque" [ref=e783]
          - StaticText " on the house at 43 Adlington Road, "
          - link "Wilmslow" [ref=e784]
          - StaticText ", where Turing lived and died"
          - superscript
            - link "[200]" [ref=e1103]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "200"
                - StaticText "]"
      - paragraph
        - StaticText "On 8 June 1954, at his house at 43 Adlington Road, "
        - link "Wilmslow" [ref=e443]
        - StaticText ", Turing's housekeeper found him dead."
        - superscript
          - link "[200]" [ref=e785]
            - generic
              - StaticText "["
              - StaticText "200"
              - StaticText "]"
        - StaticText " A post mortem was held that evening, which determined that he had died the previous day at age 41 with "
        - link "cyanide poisoning" [ref=e444]
        - StaticText " cited as the cause of death."
        - superscript
          - link "[201]" [ref=e786]
            - generic
              - StaticText "["
              - StaticText "201"
              - StaticText "]"
        - superscript
          - link "[202]" [ref=e787]
            - generic
              - StaticText "["
              - StaticText "202"
              - StaticText "]"
        - StaticText " When his body was discovered, an apple lay half-eaten beside his bed, and although the apple was not tested for cyanide,"
        - superscript
          - link "[203]" [ref=e788]
            - generic
              - StaticText "["
              - StaticText "203"
              - StaticText "]"
        - StaticText " it was speculated that this was the means by which Turing had consumed a fatal dose."
      - paragraph
        - StaticText "Turing's brother, John, identified the body the following day and took the advice given by Franz Greenbaum to accept the verdict of the "
        - link "inquest" [ref=e445]
        - StaticText ", as there was little prospect of establishing that the death was accidental."
        - superscript
          - link "[204]" [ref=e789]
            - generic
              - StaticText "["
              - StaticText "204"
              - StaticText "]"
        - StaticText " The inquest was held the following day, which determined the cause of death to be suicide."
        - superscript
          - link "[185]" [ref=e790]
            - generic
              - StaticText "["
              - StaticText "185"
              - StaticText "]"
      - paragraph
        - StaticText "Turing's remains were cremated at "
        - link "Woking Crematorium" [ref=e446]
        - StaticText " just two days later on 12 June 1954, with just his mother, brother, and "
        - link "Lyn Newman" [ref=e447]
        - StaticText " attending,"
        - superscript
          - link "[205]" [ref=e791]
            - generic
              - StaticText "["
              - StaticText "205"
              - StaticText "]"
        - superscript
          - link "[206]" [ref=e792]
            - generic
              - StaticText "["
              - StaticText "206"
              - StaticText "]"
        - StaticText " and his ashes were scattered in the gardens of the crematorium, just as his father's had been."
        - superscript
          - link "[207]" [ref=e793]
            - generic
              - StaticText "["
              - StaticText "207"
              - StaticText "]"
        - StaticText " Turing's mother was on holiday in Italy at the time of his death and returned home after the inquest. She never accepted the verdict of suicide."
        - superscript
          - link "[204]" [ref=e794]
            - generic
              - StaticText "["
              - StaticText "204"
              - StaticText "]"
      - paragraph
        - StaticText "Hodges and a later biographer, "
        - link "David Leavitt" [ref=e448]
        - StaticText ", have both speculated that Turing was re-enacting a scene from the "
        - link "Walt Disney" [ref=e449]
        - StaticText " film "
        - link "Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs" [ref=e795]
        - StaticText " (1937), his favourite fairy tale. Both men noted that (in Leavitt's words) he took \"an especially keen pleasure in the scene where the Wicked Queen immerses her apple in the poisonous brew\"."
        - superscript
          - link "[208]" [ref=e796]
            - generic
              - StaticText "["
              - StaticText "208"
              - StaticText "]"
        - superscript
          - link "[209]" [ref=e797]
            - generic
              - StaticText "["
              - StaticText "209"
              - StaticText "]"
        - superscript
          - link "[210]" [ref=e798]
            - generic
              - StaticText "["
              - StaticText "210"
              - StaticText "]"
      - figure
        - link [ref=e450]
          - image
        - Figcaption
          - StaticText "Turing's OBE currently held in "
          - link "Sherborne School" [ref=e799]
          - StaticText " archives"
      - paragraph
        - StaticText "It has also been suggested that Turing's belief in "
        - link "fortune-telling" [ref=e451]
        - StaticText " may have caused his depressed mood."
        - superscript
          - link "[207]" [ref=e800]
            - generic
              - StaticText "["
              - StaticText "207"
              - StaticText "]"
        - StaticText " As a youth, Turing had been told by a fortune-teller that he would be a genius. In mid-May 1954, shortly before his death, Turing again decided to consult a fortune-teller during a day-trip to "
        - link "St Annes-on-Sea" [ref=e452]
        - StaticText " with the Greenbaum family."
        - superscript
          - link "[207]" [ref=e801]
            - generic
              - StaticText "["
              - StaticText "207"
              - StaticText "]"
        - StaticText " According to the Greenbaums' daughter, Barbara:"
        - superscript
          - link "[193]" [ref=e802]
            - generic
              - StaticText "["
              - StaticText "193"
              - StaticText "]"
      - blockquote
        - paragraph
          - StaticText "But it was a lovely sunny day and Alan was in a cheerful mood and off we went ... Then he thought it would be a good idea to go to the "
          - link "Pleasure Beach at Blackpool" [ref=e803]
          - StaticText ". We found a fortune-teller's tent and Alan said he'd like to go in[,] so we waited around for him to come back ... And this sunny, cheerful visage had shrunk into a pale, shaking, horror-stricken face. Something had happened. We don't know what the fortune-teller said but he obviously was deeply unhappy. I think that was probably the last time we saw him before we heard of his suicide."
      - region "Doubts on suicide thesis" [ref=e176]
        - heading "Doubts on suicide thesis" [level=3, ref=e453]
        - paragraph
          - StaticText "Turing's nephew, writer Dermot Turing, does not believe that his conviction or hormone treatment had anything to do with his suicide. He pointed out that the conviction ended in 1952 and the treatment the following year. Furthermore, no physiological evidence was found that the treatment had any impact on his uncle's mental health, and he had just made a list of tasks he needed to perform when he got back to his office after a public holiday."
          - superscript
            - link "[211]" [ref=e1104]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "211"
                - StaticText "]"
          - superscript
            - link "[212]" [ref=e1105]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "212"
                - StaticText "]"
          - superscript
            - link "[87]" [ref=e1106]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "87"
                - StaticText "]"
          - StaticText " Turing may have inhaled "
          - link "potassium cyanide" [ref=e804]
          - StaticText " fumes from an "
          - link "electroplating" [ref=e805]
          - StaticText " experiment in his spare room, and he often ate an apple before bed, leaving it half eaten."
          - superscript
            - link "[211]" [ref=e1107]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "211"
                - StaticText "]"
        - paragraph
          - StaticText "Philosopher "
          - link "Jack Copeland" [ref=e806]
          - StaticText " also questioned various aspects of the coroner's historical verdict, likewise suggesting the accidental inhalation of cyanide fumes from an apparatus used to "
          - link "electroplate" [ref=e807]
          - StaticText " gold onto spoons. Copeland noted that the autopsy findings were more consistent with inhalation than with ingestion of the poison and cited his habit of eating an apple before bedtime."
          - superscript
            - link "[1]" [ref=e1108]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "1"
                - StaticText "]"
          - StaticText " Furthermore, Turing had reportedly borne his legal setbacks and hormone treatment (which had been discontinued a year previously) \"with good humour\" and had shown no sign of despondency before his death. He even set down a list of tasks that he intended to complete upon returning to his office after the holiday weekend."
          - superscript
            - link "[1]" [ref=e1109]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "1"
                - StaticText "]"
          - StaticText " Turing's mother believed that the ingestion was accidental, resulting from her son's careless storage of laboratory chemicals."
          - superscript
            - link "[213]" [ref=e1110]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "213"
                - StaticText "]"
          - StaticText " Turing biographer "
          - link "Andrew Hodges" [ref=e808]
          - StaticText " theorised that Turing deliberately made his death look accidental to shield his mother from the knowledge that he had killed himself."
          - superscript
            - link "[214]" [ref=e1111]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "214"
                - StaticText "]"
        - paragraph
          - StaticText "Doubts on the suicide thesis have been also cast by "
          - link "John W. Dawson Jr." [ref=e809]
          - StaticText " who, in his review of Hodges' book, recalls \"Turing's vulnerable position in the Cold War political climate\" and points out that \"Turing was found dead by a maid, who discovered him 'lying neatly in his bed'—hardly what one would expect of \"a man fighting for life against the suffocation induced by cyanide poisoning.\" Turing had given no hint of suicidal inclinations to his friends and had made no effort to put his affairs in order."
          - superscript
            - link "[215]" [ref=e1112]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "215"
                - StaticText "]"
    - region "Government apology and pardon" [ref=e141]
      - heading "Government apology and pardon" [level=2, ref=e177]
      - note
        - StaticText "Further information: "
        - link "Alan Turing law" [ref=e454]
      - paragraph
        - StaticText "In August 2009, British programmer "
        - link "John Graham-Cumming" [ref=e455]
        - StaticText " started a petition urging the British government to apologise for Turing's prosecution as a homosexual."
        - superscript
          - link "[216]" [ref=e810]
            - generic
              - StaticText "["
              - StaticText "216"
              - StaticText "]"
        - superscript
          - link "[217]" [ref=e811]
            - generic
              - StaticText "["
              - StaticText "217"
              - StaticText "]"
        - StaticText " The petition received more than 30,000 signatures."
        - superscript
          - link "[218]" [ref=e812]
            - generic
              - StaticText "["
              - StaticText "218"
              - StaticText "]"
        - superscript
          - link "[219]" [ref=e813]
            - generic
              - StaticText "["
              - StaticText "219"
              - StaticText "]"
        - StaticText " The prime minister, "
        - link "Gordon Brown" [ref=e456]
        - StaticText ", acknowledged the petition, releasing a statement on 10 September 2009 apologising and describing the treatment of Turing as \"appalling\":"
        - superscript
          - link "[218]" [ref=e814]
            - generic
              - StaticText "["
              - StaticText "218"
              - StaticText "]"
        - superscript
          - link "[220]" [ref=e815]
            - generic
              - StaticText "["
              - StaticText "220"
              - StaticText "]"
      - blockquote
        - paragraph
          - StaticText "Thousands of people have come together to demand justice for Alan Turing and recognition of the appalling way he was treated. While Turing was dealt with under the law of the time and we can't put the clock back, his treatment was of course utterly unfair and I am pleased to have the chance to say how deeply sorry I and we all are for what happened to him ... So on behalf of the British government, and all those who live freely thanks to Alan's work I am very proud to say: we're sorry, you deserved so much better."
          - superscript
            - link "[218]" [ref=e1113]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "218"
                - StaticText "]"
          - superscript
            - link "[221]" [ref=e1114]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "221"
                - StaticText "]"
      - paragraph
        - StaticText "In December 2011, William Jones and his member of Parliament, "
        - link "John Leech" [ref=e457]
        - StaticText ", created an "
        - link "e-petition" [ref=e458]
        - superscript
          - link "[222]" [ref=e816]
            - generic
              - StaticText "["
              - StaticText "222"
              - StaticText "]"
        - StaticText " requesting that the British government "
        - link "pardon" [ref=e459]
        - StaticText " Turing for his conviction of \"gross indecency\":"
        - superscript
          - link "[223]" [ref=e817]
            - generic
              - StaticText "["
              - StaticText "223"
              - StaticText "]"
      - blockquote
        - paragraph
          - StaticText "We ask the HM Government to grant a pardon to Alan Turing for the conviction of \"gross indecency\". In 1952, he was convicted of \"gross indecency\" with another man and was forced to undergo so-called \"organo-therapy\"—chemical castration. Two years later, he killed himself with cyanide, aged just 41. Alan Turing was driven to a terrible despair and early death by the nation he'd done so much to save. This remains a shame on the British government and British history. A pardon can go some way to healing this damage. It may act as an apology to many of the other gay men, not as well-known as Alan Turing, who were subjected to these laws."
          - superscript
            - link "[222]" [ref=e1115]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "222"
                - StaticText "]"
      - paragraph
        - StaticText "The petition gathered over 37,000 signatures,"
        - superscript
          - link "[222]" [ref=e818]
            - generic
              - StaticText "["
              - StaticText "222"
              - StaticText "]"
        - superscript
          - link "[224]" [ref=e819]
            - generic
              - StaticText "["
              - StaticText "224"
              - StaticText "]"
        - StaticText " and was submitted to Parliament by the Manchester MP John Leech but the request was discouraged by Justice Minister "
        - link "Lord McNally" [ref=e460]
        - StaticText ", who said:"
        - superscript
          - link "[225]" [ref=e820]
            - generic
              - StaticText "["
              - StaticText "225"
              - StaticText "]"
      - blockquote
        - paragraph
          - StaticText "A posthumous pardon was not considered appropriate as Alan Turing was properly convicted of what at the time was a criminal offence. He would have known that his offence was against the law and that he would be prosecuted. It is tragic that Alan Turing was convicted of an offence that now seems both cruel and absurd—particularly poignant given his outstanding contribution to the war effort. However, the law at the time required a prosecution and, as such, long-standing policy has been to accept that such convictions took place and, rather than trying to alter the historical context and to put right what cannot be put right, ensure instead that we never again return to those times."
          - superscript
            - link "[226]" [ref=e1116]
              - generic
                - StaticText "["
                - StaticText "226"
                - StaticText "]"
      - paragraph
        - StaticText "John Leech, the MP for "
        - link "Manchester Withington" [ref=e461]
        - StaticText " (2005–15), submitted several bills to Parliament"
        - superscript
          - link "[227]" [ref=e821]
            - generic
              - StaticText "["
              - StaticText "227"
              - StaticText "]"
        - StaticText " and led a high-profile campaign to secure the pardon. Leech made the case in the House of Commons that Turing's contribution to the war made him a national hero and that it was \"ultimately just embarrassing\" that the conviction still stood."
        - superscript
          - link "[228]" [ref=e822]
            - generic
              - StaticText "["
              - StaticText "228"
              - StaticText "]"
        - StaticText " Leech continued to take the bill through Parliament and campaigned for several years, gaining the public support of numerous leading scientists, including the physicist "
        - link "Stephen Hawking" [ref=e462]
        - StaticText "."
        - superscript
          - link "[229]" [ref=e823]
            - generic
              - StaticText "["
              - StaticText "229"
              - StaticText "]"
        - superscript
          - link "[230]" [ref=e824]
            - generic
              - StaticText "["
              - StaticText "230"
              - StaticText "]"
      - paragraph
        - StaticText "On 25 July 2012, a bill was introduced in the "
        - link "House of Lords" [ref=e463]
        - StaticText " by "
        - link "Lord Sharkey" [ref=e464]
        - StaticText " to grant a statutory pardon to Turing for offences under section 11 of the Criminal Law Amendment Act 1885, of which he was convicted on 31 March 1952."
        - superscript
          - link "[231]" [ref=e825]
            - generic
              - StaticText "["
              - StaticText "231"
              - StaticText "]"
        - StaticText " In December of that year, in a letter to "
        - link "The Daily Telegraph" [ref=e826]
        - StaticText ", Hawking and 10 other signatories including the "
        - link "Astronomer Royal" [ref=e465]
        - link "Lord Rees" [ref=e466]
        - StaticText ", "
        - link "President of the Royal Society" [ref=e467]
        - StaticText " Sir "
        - link "Paul Nurse" [ref=e468]
        - StaticText ", "
        - link "Lady Trumpington" [ref=e469]
        - StaticText " (who worked for Turing during the war) and Lord Sharkey (the bill's sponsor) called on Prime Minister "
        - link "David Cameron" [ref=e470]
        - StaticText " to act on the pardon request."
        - superscript
          - link "[232]" [ref=e827]
            - generic
              - StaticText "["
              - StaticText "232"
              - StaticText "]"
        - StaticText " Lord Sharkey's bill did not progress past the 1st reading stage in the House of Lords during the 2012-2013 parliamentary session,"
        - superscript
          - link "[231]" [ref=e828]
            - generic
              - StaticText "["
              - StaticText "231"
              - StaticText "]"
        - StaticText " and was subsequently reintroduced at the start of the next session on 9 May 2013, co-sponsored by Leech."
        - superscript
          - link "[233]" [ref=e829]
            - generic
              - StaticText "["
              - StaticText "233"
              - StaticText "]"
        - StaticText " On 19 July 2013, the day of the second reading in the Lords, the government indicated that it would support the bill."
        - superscript
          - link "[234]" [ref=e830]
            - generic
              - StaticText "["
              - StaticText "234"
              - StaticText "]"
        - StaticText " It passed its third reading in the Lords on 30 October,"
        - superscript
          - link "[233]" [ref=e831]
            - generic
              - StaticText "["
              - StaticText "233"
              - StaticText "]"
        - superscript
          - link "[235]" [ref=e832]
            - generic
              - StaticText "["
              - StaticText "235"
              - StaticText "]"
        - superscript
          - link "[236]" [ref=e833]
            - generic
              - StaticText "["
              - StaticText "236"
              - StaticText "]"
        - StaticText " with its first reading in the "
        - link "House of Commons" [ref=e471]
        - StaticText " occurring on the same day."
        - superscript
          - link "[233]" [ref=e834]
            - generic
              - StaticText "["
              - StaticText "233"
              - StaticText "]"
      - paragraph
        - StaticText "At the bill's second reading in the Commons on 29 November 2013, Conservative MP "
        - link "Christopher Chope" [ref=e472]
        - StaticText " objected to the bill, delaying its passage."
        - superscript
          - link "[235]" [ref=e835]
            - generic
              - StaticText "["
              - StaticText "235"
              - StaticText "]"
        - StaticText " The bill was due to return to the Commons on 28 February 2014,"
        - superscript
          - link "[235]" [ref=e836]
            - generic
              - StaticText "["
              - StaticText "235"
              - StaticText "]"
        - StaticText " but before the bill could be debated, the government elected to proceed instead under the "
        - link "royal prerogative of mercy" [ref=e473]
        - StaticText ". On 24 December 2013, "
        - link "Queen Elizabeth II" [ref=e474]
        - StaticText " signed a "
        - link "royal warrant" [ref=e475]
        - StaticText ", "
        - link "pardoning" [ref=e476]
        - StaticText " for Turing's conviction for \"gross indecency\", with immediate effect."
        - superscript
          - link "[237]" [ref=e837]
            - generic
              - StaticText "["
              - StaticText "237"
              - StaticText "]"
        - superscript
          - link "[238]" [ref=e838]
            - generic
              - StaticText "["
              - StaticText "238"
              - StaticText "]"
        - StaticText " Announcing the pardon, Lord Chancellor "
        - link "Chris Grayling" [ref=e477]
        - StaticText " said Turing deserved to be \"remembered and recognised for his fantastic contribution to the war effort\" and not for his later criminal conviction."
        - superscript
          - link "[224]" [ref=e839]
            - generic
              - StaticText "["
              - StaticText "224"
              - StaticText "]"
        - superscript
          - link "[239]" [ref=e840]
            - generic
              - StaticText "["
              - StaticText "239"
              - StaticText "]"
        - StaticText " It was only the fourth royal pardon granted since the conclusion of the Second World War."
        - superscript
          - link "[240]" [ref=e841]
            - generic
              - StaticText "["
              - StaticText "240"
              - StaticText "]"
        - StaticText " Pardons are normally granted only when the person is technically innocent, and a request has been made by the family or other interested party; neither condition was met in regard to Turing's conviction."
        - superscript
          - link "[241]" [ref=e842]
            - generic
              - StaticText "["
              - StaticText "241"
              - StaticText "]"
      - paragraph
        - StaticText "In September 2016, the government announced its intention to expand this retroactive exoneration to other men convicted of similar historical indecency offences, in what was described as an \""
        - link "Alan Turing law" [ref=e478]
        - StaticText "\"."
        - superscript
          - link "[242]" [ref=e843]
            - generic
              - StaticText "["
              - StaticText "242"
              - StaticText "]"
        - superscript
          - link "[243]" [ref=e844]
            - generic
              - StaticText "["
              - StaticText "243"
              - StaticText "]"
        - StaticText " The Alan Turing law is now an informal term for the law in the United Kingdom, contained in the "
        - link "Policing and Crime Act 2017" [ref=e479]
        - StaticText ", which serves as an "
        - link "amnesty law" [ref=e480]
        - StaticText " to retroactively pardon men who were cautioned or convicted under historical legislation that outlawed homosexual acts. The law applies in England and Wales."
        - superscript
          - link "[244]" [ref=e845]
            - generic
              - StaticText "["
              - StaticText "244"
              - StaticText "]"
        - StaticText " Due to his repeated attempts to bring attention to the issue, Leech is now regularly described as the \"architect\" of Turing's pardon and subsequently the Alan Turing Law, which went on to secure pardons for 75,000 other men and women."
        - superscript
          - link "[245]" [ref=e846]
            - generic
              - StaticText "["
              - StaticText "245"
              - StaticText "]"
        - superscript
          - link "[246]" [ref=e847]
            - generic
              - StaticText "["
              - StaticText "246"
              - StaticText "]"
        - superscript
          - link "[247]" [ref=e848]
            - generic
              - StaticText "["
              - StaticText "247"
              - StaticText "]"
        - StaticText " At the British premiere of a film based on Turing's life, "
        - link "The Imitation Game" [ref=e849]
        - StaticText ", the producers thanked Leech for bringing the topic to public attention and securing Turing's pardon."
        - superscript
          - link "[248]" [ref=e850]
            - generic
              - StaticText "["
              - StaticText "248"
              - StaticText "]"
      - paragraph
        - StaticText "On 19 July 2023, following "
        - link "an apology to LGBT veterans" [ref=e481]
        - StaticText " from the UK Government, "
        - link "Defence Secretary" [ref=e482]
        - link "Ben Wallace" [ref=e483]
        - StaticText " suggested Turing should be honoured with a permanent statue on the "
        - link "fourth plinth of Trafalgar Square" [ref=e484]
        - StaticText ", describing Turing as \"probably the greatest war hero, in my book, of the Second World War, [whose] achievements shortened the war, saved thousands of lives, helped defeat the Nazis. And his story is a sad story of a society and how it treated him.\""
        - superscript
          - link "[249]" [ref=e851]
            - generic
              - StaticText "["
              - StaticText "249"
              - StaticText "]"
        - superscript
          - link "[250]" [ref=e852]
            - generic
              - StaticText "["
              - StaticText "250"
              - StaticText "]"
        - superscript
          - link "[251]" [ref=e853]
            - generic
              - StaticText "["
              - StaticText "251"
              - StaticText "]"

              - generic
                - StaticText "\""
                - StaticText "In late 1940 Alan Turing wrote a report describing the methods he and his colleagues at Bletchley Park had used to break into the German Enigma cipher systems. At Bletchley it was known as 'the Prof's Book.' A copy of this handbook was at last released from secrecy by the American National Security Agency in April 1996, under the title "
                - StaticText "Turing's Treatise on the Enigma"
                - StaticText ". Subsequently, a much better original copy was released by the (British) National Archives, box HW 25/3. This also revealed a title which had been lost in the American copy: "
                - StaticText "Mathematical theory of ENIGMA machine"
                - StaticText ". (Though, oddly, the report does not actually have any mathematical theory.)"
